tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) paper ('Benchmarking Learned Indexes'). Its Table 2 lists RS at 266.58 ns / 4.0 MB against the STX B+ Tree [6] at 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, and the setup section states the CPU (Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz, 256 GB RAM). The SOSD harness is public (learnedsystems/SOSD, benchmarks/ + scripts/prepare.sh + CMakeLists.txt), but neither the paper nor the repo pins a compiler, so it cannot be A.

corrections.workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn (books) dataset of 200M keys. Table 2 specifically uses a 32-bit version of amzn and reports the best-performing (often largest) variant of each index structure, comparing RadixSpline (RS) against the STX B+ Tree, IBTree, FAST, binary search, PGM, RMI, CuckooMap and RobinHash. The Pareto plots (Fig. 7) cover 64-bit keys over amzn/face/osm/wiki.
corrections.claimed_speedup: 266.58 ns/lookup (4.0 MB) for RS vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree (STX B+ Tree) on the 32-bit version of the amzn dataset, fastest variant of each -> ~1.8x lower latency at ~41x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SOSD repo build (scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt) uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, -ffast-math -march=native, and -fopenmp if available. The compiler is not pinned; the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04.
corrections.caveats: Same SOSD/VLDB'21 paper as the RMI entry. The CPU is stated and the SOSD harness is public, but no compiler is named (flags only in the SOSD CMake build), so it is capped at Tier B. Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn and are the fastest variant per structure. RS beats PGM (326.48 ns) but trails RMI (180.90 ns), and both hash tables (CuckooMap 114.50 ns, RobinHash 93.69 ns) beat every ordered index at far larger size. RS and RBS degrade badly on the face dataset because of outliers. It is a header-only C++ library whose last commit on master is 2021-05-13 (the 2023-04-28 date is only the repo pushed_at). The SOSD harness itself is GPL-3.0, while the RS library is MIT.

notes: Numbers and the STX B-Tree baseline check out, but Table 2 is explicitly on a 32-bit version of amzn, not the 64-bit keys the record claimed; I fixed the workload. last_commit was the repo pushed_at; the real last commit on master is 2021-05-13, so it is still abandoned. License MIT, 141 stars, not a fork and not archived were all verified.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) paper. Its Table 2 lists RMI at 180.90 ns / 48.0 MB against the STX B+ Tree at 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, and the setup section states a Xeon Gold 6230 CPU. The SOSD harness is public (learnedsystems/SOSD benchmarks/, scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt with -ffast-math -march=native in a Release build), but no compiler is named, so it cannot be A.

corrections.workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn (books) dataset of 200M keys. Table 2 specifically uses a 32-bit version of amzn and reports the best-performing (often largest) variant of each index structure, comparing a CDFShop-tuned RMI against the STX B+ Tree, IBTree, FAST, binary search, PGM, RadixSpline, CuckooMap and RobinHash. The Pareto plots (Fig. 7) cover 64-bit keys over amzn/face/osm/wiki.
corrections.claimed_speedup: 180.90 ns/lookup (48.0 MB) for RMI vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree (STX B+ Tree) on the 32-bit version of the amzn dataset, fastest variant of each -> ~2.7x lower latency at ~3.5x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SOSD repo build (scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt) uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, -ffast-math -march=native, and -fopenmp if available; the RMI code is generated by the Rust compiler (cargo). The C++ compiler is not pinned; the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04.
corrections.caveats: The SOSD/VLDB'21 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' paper states the CPU model and methodology, and the SOSD harness is public, but no compiler is named, so it is capped at Tier B. Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn and are the fastest (48 MB) RMI variant. Both hash tables (CuckooMap 114.50 ns / 1541 MB, RobinHash 93.69 ns / 6144 MB) are faster for point lookups. RMIs are read-only, need offline training, and take much longer to build than PGM/RS or B-Trees (Section 4.6). The RMI 'library' is a Rust compiler that emits C/C++ source files, and those generated files are what gets linked and benchmarked. The SOSD harness is GPL-3.0, while the RMI repo is MIT.

notes: Numbers and the STX B-Tree baseline are confirmed in Table 2, but that table is on a 32-bit version of amzn, so I corrected the workload. Metadata checks out: MIT, 239 stars, not a fork and not archived, last commit 2026-05-27 (merge of PR #7), so active is correct. The language field says Rust, which is accurate for the generator, but the benchmarked artifact is generated C++.
